title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I was hesitant to buy this speaker for my Dell U2415 monitor based on so many reviews that said it didn't work as advertised (i.e. that it needed both a USB connection for power as well as an aux cable for the sound signal "THAT ISN'T EVEN INCLUDED!!!). Some folks even said that it didn't work with both a USB and aux cable connected.
But I wanted a speaker that wouldn't take up any space on my desk and I don't need disco club volume nor thumping base, so I went for it. I figured worst case I'd need to use an aux cable (or worst worst-case it wouldn't work for me at all and I have to return it, but hey, returning stuff is one of Amazon's strengths, right?)
So anyway it delivered next day after ordering (the joys of living in a metropolitan area!), I pulled it out of the box and connected the speaker's USB cable into one of the monitor's USB hub outlets and voila, sound was coming out of the speaker even before Skype and all of the other annoying Microsoft bloat-ware had finished starting up after I powered my computer on. Absolutely no setup of any sort required from me on the computer side of things. See the attached picture to this review for how the computer shows the speaker in the audio output section after all is said and done. So easy and I'm running Windows 8 on this machine, for Pete's Sake!

Which leads me to wonder; do people not realize that if you plug this speaker's USB plug into one of the monitor's USB ports that the monitor itself has to ALSO be connected to the computer independently via its own USB cord?
Even if you don't have your monitor hub connected (or don't have a monitor hub at all), the attached USB plug on the speaker has quite a long cord so hypothetically it would easily plug directly into the computer itself. I haven't tried that, but am absolutely confident it would work just fine. Even better, theoretically, since plugging the speaker into the monitor USB port instead of the computer's means the audio has the extra complexity of going through the USB hub in the monitor. Not that I've noticed any problems at all with that but I suppose if you were doing high data-rate transfers through the hub the sound could take a hit because of it.

Sound is perfectly fine, even great, for the size and price of this thing. Again, I don't need disco club volume nor thumping base nor battlefield realistic sound for my application so you may feel differently.
Actually I had to lower the speaker, computer, and music app volumes all down to the lower ends of their respective sliders while playing some test tracks since my kid's bedroom is right next to my "office" and the sound output was pretty significant when I first plugged it in.

My U2415 has two slots in the bottom of it that were covered up with some glorified tape pieces. Once I pulled the tape off with a mini-screwdriver the two tabs on top of the speaker slotted right into the monitor slots and it looks just like one of the photos Amazon has posted for this item.

If you go to Dell's page for this speaker, click on the "Tech Specs" tab, and scroll down to "Compatibility" you'll see a long list of Dell monitors this speaker is designed to work with. I'd guesstimate 2 out of 3 or maybe even 4 out of 5 in that list don't need the included monitor stand mount (the list differentiates which do or don't). Mine was one of those that don't so I can't speak to people's issues with the monitor stand mount, but I'm wondering if their monitor is even on that list at all.

I got this for a desktop computer I was building and added it under my Dell monitor. I use it for conference calls, not for music. It plays music just fine and plenty loud but it is a soundbar. Sounds: Voices are loud and clear for calls. The soundbar has volume adjust buttons which increase or decrease the Windows volume control. The sound is a bit deeper and richer than you get from typical "tinny" sounding PC speakers. I have not run into any issues with audio.

Mic: This unit has an integrated far-field microphone. I typically sit 2-4 feet from the microphone and it picks my voice up well. Feedback has been that I sound clear on calls. There is a mute button on the soundbar, in addition to buttons for answer and hang-up, which could be handy in certain circumstances. The microphone on this soundbar is far better than the integrated mic on my USB camera. However, I would say it's generally of average sound capture quality. I have had no issues with it and it is sufficient for hours of daily conference calls.

I have attached pictures of the front view under monitor and the rear view of the mounting adapter.

I purchased this because it had an integrated microphone. I believe that is the key feature to choose this soundbar over all other alternatives available. The second feature would be mounting compatibility with Dell monitors. The third feature would be the inclusion of front mounted buttons for volume, mute, and call handling if someone were looking for a setup without easy access to a keyboard or mouse (i.e. distributed setup or TV display as a conferencing interface).

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Dell USB DVD Read Write DW216. Upon plugging provided cable and drive into computer, the drive functioned as a plug and play device on Microsoft Surface laptop running Windows 11 64 bit. Device manager, file explorer, and media software functioned normally. Surprisingly, the drive functioned normally on computer battery alone.

Provided CyberLink Media Suite 12 disc did not auto run as Windows blocked installation requiring Administrator access even though I am the administrator for the computer. I used/mixed two suggestions found in these Amazon reviews to install the Suite. 1. In the search bar, I typed "command prompt" and then clicked "Run as Administrator" on the right side of window. 2. In the command prompt window, I typed "net user administrator /active:yes" (exactly - keeping the spaces in between words & symbols) and tapped enter. 3. The computer replied "The command completed successfully". 4. I determined the drive letter of the DW316 in file explorer. I right clicked on the drive and selected properties to see the drive letter. 5. In the command window, I typed the drive letter and a colon sign and tapped enter. 6. I typed "cd cms" and tapped enter. 7. I typed setup.exe and tapped enter. 8. From this point the software installation process started. 9. After installation, at the command prompt, I typed "net user administrator /active:no" and tapped enter which was followed by the message "The command completed successfully" to take the computer out of administrator access. Good luck.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
So far, so good. Initially connected with Ubuntu Gnome 16.04 on a Broadwell Dell notebook, and it was terrible- a torturous, tearing fiasco like you can't believe.

Tested briefly with a Win 10 laptop (Ivy Bridge hp ProBook 6470b), and it automagically downloaded everything it needed within a couple minutes, and all was well. I decided to fetch the latest dock driver from Dell's website and push it onto the device while I had the Windows notebook plugged in. No apparent change. Switching back to Gnome afterwards was still unbearable.

So I did apt install xfce4, rebooted into XFCE, and it works really well. Tried again with clean installation of Ubuntu 16.04.1 ("normal", with Unity), and it worked surprisingly well too. I don't know what the deal was with Gnome being so awful. It's a shame, too, since I really like Gnome, and it's what I always use on my CentOS and Fedora installations.

Dock is currently connecting AmazonBasics A100 USB-powered speakers (consuming a USB 3.0 port and an audio jack), two external 1080p monitors over HDMI, and a USB keyboard and mouse over the two USB 2.0 ports. All is working as expected. I may check back in a few days after I add my third monitor.

This setup appears to have very little discernible CPU penalty.

Cool bit of kit. Kind of dense for its size, and the underside creates enough friction to keep her pretty still on a desk. Well thought out.

02.06.2017 udpate: I had trouble adding a third external display (all three external monitors are matching 1080p ViewSonic). Can't recall error message, but I couldn't populate the display on a third monitor. I just worked around the issue by running HDMI directly from laptop to one of the external monitors, and I let the D3100 feed the other two (one via HDMI, the other uses a Displayport-to-HDMI adapter for the moment). Just note you may have a problem with three displays.

Currently: Ubuntu 16.04 on Dell 5548 notebook, fully patched, tested with and without Intel-proprietary drivers, stock 4.4 kernel. I'm satisfied with the setup, and I don't intend to fiddle with it any further.

03/2017 update:
Inconsistent results coming up from sleep state or reboot. Got tired of fussing, so I sold the thing. I'll never buy a consumer-type notebook again, only business-class kit from now on. A proper dock and a computer with proper dock support is worth the spend, to me.

text:
Ich habe mir diese Dock bestellt da ich es mit meinem Tablet (Acer Iconia W700) auch als Desktop-Rechner nutzen wollte.
Dafür brauchte ich natürlich mehr USB-Anschlüsse (Maus + Tastatur, Webcam, DVD-RW-Laufwerk, USB-Stick...).
Zudem hatte ich auch keine Lust jedes mal HDMI-Kabel, 3,5-Klinkenstecker, USB-Hub und Netzstecker an und ab zu stöpseln. Daher habe ich nach einiger Recherche das Dell D3100 bestellt.

Zum Dock selbst:
- Gut verarbeitet
- Kompakt
- Anschlüsse sind gut verteilt und in ausreichender Zahl vorhanden
- von Lüftergeräuschen oder großer Hitzeentwicklung ist nichts zu merken

Zur Funktion:
- Aufbau, Verkabelung, usw. - alles sehr einfach

- Audio, USB-Geräte, LAN - alles läuft super

Monitor:
- Auflösung bei mir Full-HD
- per DVI und per HDMI läuft einwandfrei - ich habe den Monitor über ein HDMI-Kabel angeschlossen
- ob und wie es mit zwei Monitoren HD oder 4K aussieht kann ich nicht sagen, da ich dies noch nicht probiert habe

Von Verzögerungen beim Bild oder verschlechterter Qualität habe ich nichts gemerkt, auch nicht bei HD-Filmen. Spiele von der Xbox One auf das Tablet und somit über die Dock auf den Monitor läuft auch super. text:

I needed to replace a broken mouse for my home computer. The one that I used to have doesn't seem to be available any longer.

I was looking for an inexpensive basic 3-button wired mouse that is comfortable to use all day long. I like big mice, to put all my hand on in a relaxed position, and not have to clutch it. After trying out several different ones, which were adequate but still not what I was looking for, I got myself the same mouse that is provided for me in my office, and I love it.

It is reasonably large - well, at least it is hard to find a larger one which also has other features I was looking for. It is simple not only in the sense of being a 3-button no-frills wired mouse, but also in the design made of straight parallel lines with a round wheel and a low profile. It doesn't make claims of being ergonomic, but it is very comfortable for my hand, placing all the fingers where they are supposed to be, and I easily move it with just my fingers, leaving my wrist rest on the desk, just the way I like it. It doesn't make claims of being noiseless, but it is reasonably quiet - not completely silent, but providing a relatively low clicking feedback sound that doesn't bother me at all. It works well without a mouse pad, so I don't need to clutter my precious desk real estate with it. Haven't experienced any problems with this mouse at home or in the office, it just works.

This one is a keeper.

text:
Dell AC511 USB Wired SoundBar ... by Dell

IN THE BOX ... was the Dell AC511 USB wired SoundBAR, and a USB (male to Femaile) extender. The Dell AC511 is packaged in a heavy corregated box by the manufacturer and shipped inside a shipping box.

CONDITION AND OPERATION... is very good. The Dell AC511 is brand new and was designed to work with designated DELL monitors. Overlooking the design intent, I have used the DELL AC511 on my Dell 755 SFE and my Lenovo laptop. There is no power supply, the power is supplied through the USB cord. There is NO AUX JACK. Only the USB connection.
... The AC511 bypasses your sound card and you don't need any additonal software.
... If you dont have sound, look at your sound source in your computer. Should list the AC511 as a selection. True with Linux systems as well.
... If the sound is noisey, or scratchy, which may happen if plugged into the monitor, try a different USB port, try a port on the computer.
... The AC511 has head phone jacks on the side. If the jacks are noisy, try cleaning the jack and plug.
... The AC511 DOES NOT HAVE AN AUX JACK to plug in a MiniDisc player or MP3 player. Does not have that capability. Only USB input.
... The AC511 was designed to work on designated DELL monitors because DELL installed a USB port for the soundbar on the monitor. However, the AC511 does work on most computers with a USB port.

THE LAST WORD ... The Dell AC511 has a pretty good sound for a small-ish sound bar. It is a quality product and may be an answer for a computer with a bad sound card as the AC511 replaces that sound card. Sound control is from the volume control on the AC511 on the side and/or from the computer volume controls. The sound is rich and good quality. the only way you will get better sound is with separate speakers and then unless you add a sub woofer, you may not experience that big of a difference.
... For a laptop with those built in speakers or a computer that needs a set of speakers, this should work fine. All you need is a USB port.
I would recommend the DELL AC511 speaker sound bar.

EDIT 071518 There are on going reports of uncontrollable static after using these speakers for awhile and I did have this happen to mine. I actually shelved these speakers for awhile because I couldn't figure out how to stop the static noise that would randomly pop up.
BUT one day I was working on a computer and just plugged one of these in for the sound. It worked with no static, and it continued to work. The only difference was the USB cable was no where near a monitor or computer except for where it plugged in.
--- one suggested fix was to put tin foil over the speaker unit, I have tried this and had some good results. But I have now found that the USB cable is acting like an antenna and will recieve signals that can trigger the stattic noise.
--- I want to make one thing clear, these are rather good sounding speakers. They sound better than my replacements when the static noise made them useless. It would be a plus to be able to get these working again.
--- I have experiemented recently by shielding the speaker box with tin foil, or you can place them under a metal container, and keeping the cord away from the monitor and the computer, and especially away from any of the other cords from the monitor and computer. I have had good results, no static. There have been many complaints to DELL and they haven't found a fix other than discontinuing the speakers. But the sound is good enough that it is worth the extra trouble to shield them to keep any outside signals from triggering that static noise which obliterates any usable sound from the speakers. Of course, pulling and replacing the USB corrects this for the moment but it will come back.
--- If you still have yours, try some shielding, These were a good idea but some spurrious signals are mucking up the output.

text:
Recently my 15 year old PC monitor with inbuilt speakers died on me. Had to get a replacement, but found that the ones with speakers were either way too big, or too expensive. I decided to get a reasonably priced one minus speakers and use a soundbar instead. Found this Dell AC511 , read the reviews and did the usual bit of research before purchasing. I have to say, its performance for the price is very, very good. However, I have to admit that I have had it unboxed, just sitting there for about a week because although I am fairly computer savvy, the instructions for setting it up were not the best, and reading through all the Amazon Q & A's, I found so many varying suggestions on connecting it - I honestly was not sure whether it connected to my monitor, or the PC, or both!! Today I decided to connect it how I thought best, because after all, this is a plug & play device. For anyone contemplating buying this soundbar, and like me, are not sure how it will connect and work, here is how I did it - absolutely simple.
It comes with a reasonably long USB lead. Put the USB into a vacant port on the back of your computer whilst it (and the monitor) is on - I have an HP desktop running Windows 7 Pro, but I am sure it will work the same with any usual operating system
Windows recognised it immediately and installed the driver.
Next, go into Start/Control panel/Hardware & Sound. At the bottom of the list you will see the Soundbar called "SRS Audio Control"
To adjust sound to where you want it to be (bass/mixer etc), click on the "SRS Audio Control" and all the settings are there relating to the device. Just adjust with the slider buttons.
You can adjust the sound via the knob on the right hand side of the bar, or via your speakers icon on your PC taskbar.
How simple is that? No configurations required, no A to B cable, no additional USB cables - just the attached USB cable the soundbar comes with.
I tested the sound with a Youtube video recording of music to get the sound I wanted, and it was excellent. Good bass - no tinniness, or distortion even when I had the speakers up louder than I would use. I found even at about 38% it was quite comfortably loud enough.
Looks unobtrusive and sleek - and most of all - absolutely does the job. You could, if you wish, pay a few hundred pounds for one, but in all honesty I am more than happy with this to say the least. Excellent piece of kit.
Arrived very quickly, and well packaged - all credit due to the Seller.
If you cannot attach it to your monitor, it will look just as smart placed in front of it at desk level (put a bit of bluetack underneath to keep it secure)
So glad I did not bother with another inbuilt speaker monitor after all - never could get such a great sound as this . produces!!

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I don't ever write reviews but this one was too good to pass.
If you're lazy, just get a supported Dell monitor these fit onto. If you already have one, more power to you.
If you don't have a supported monitor but willing to put some work, the rewards are more than worth it.

HOOKING TO THE MONITOR:
I don't have the dell monitors that these fit into so I almost didn't buy. I saw the top review that had someone use the VESA mount points to hook it onto their non-dell monitor so it completely changed my mind. Thank you stranger. I also use a mounting arm so the original stand was just sitting in my closet eating dust. After inspecting its parts, I had an idea. If I could somehow connect the part that locks to the monitor and the speaker, it should work. There had to be a 1 cm gap between the two as well. I just had to find something thin yet strong enough to hold the two together. After searching around the house, I found the perfect thing, the drip edges from my shed roof. I had some odd pieces laying around from a recent remodel. Cut two pieces, folded them, drilled a couple holes and used stapler from the stapler gun to fasten everything together and voila, my Acer monitor has a soundbar now. I can also take it out with just a push.

ELECTRICALS:
It requires a 12V power supply, and no it's not in the box. For people complaining about it not being provided, I'm sure all of us have atleast a few just laying around the house, from old routers, rokus, humidifiers, etc. If you don't, just go to your local thrift store and they will have one for like 69¢. Just make sure you confirm the polarity of the wires on DC side. Normally, ground is plain black wire and +12V has white dashed lines on top, but better to verify with a multimeter.

The power supply wire on speaker has 2 wires inside: red and black. I actually took the speaker apart to make sure red was +12V and black was ground, and yes they were. So I just had to find an adapter and hook it to my existing monitor arm setup. I took it apart, took the prongs out and soldered wires in place so I could fit it between a gap under my desk. I then spliced that AC side wire to the cable going to one of my monitors so when I switch on the monitor, the speaker also turns on (I have a separate physical master switch that makes sure the monitors are completely off the circuit and not just on standby mode). I already had a AUX cable also going through my monitor arm so I just had to get a coupler to hook the speaker. As a added bonus, the mounting bracket also doubled as a wire management thing, and you can just hook another wire in parallel from here if you add another speaker to a second monitor, no need for another adapter.

SUMMARY:
$8.80 and a couple hours of work later, my monitor has a soundbar with dedicated satisfying volume controller, two headphone plugs, and a cool light. Since it has dedicated power supplied, it gets plenty loud. These were premium speakers when they were released so I really have no issues with the sound quality. Yes, there could be a bluetooth, or a microphone input but it is what it is. As added bonus, my desk has more free space and no messy wires, and no stupid RGB lights like the other soundbars on Amazon.
Already bought two more to just keep them for future use.

I purchased this keyboard for both gaming and everyday computer use.

As an everyday keyboard, this product is perfect. It isn't obnoxiously loud and I have had no issues with keys being faulty in any way, which you would expect from a company as established as Dell. If you find the keyboard is too flat, it has flaps underneath, offering a more comfortable angle to type for long periods. The keyboard uses a USB connection to the PC with a 1m cable which is plentiful but you may want to use cable management if there is too much.

If you want to use this as a gaming keyboard, by all means, you will still enjoy gaming as much as you always have. For less than £20, don't expect reasonable responsiveness from the keys that other gaming keyboards - in higher price bands - might offer. In my opinion, being good at a game mostly comes down to the player, hence "a builder doesn't blame his tools." That said, I'm sure others are insistent that a more expensive keyboard is required to enable optimal performance, which may be the case for them.

Overall, the keyboard is an ordinary keyboard that fulfils its role as a reliable piece of hardware, The packaging didn't seem too special, but delivery has no complaints. If you're a starting PC gamer or just need something that is compatible with your PC, I would wholeheartedly recommend this product,

I like Dell equipment. My work laptop is Dell. My gaming PC is Dell Alienware. Love them. So, I spent about 30% more on this Dell mouse and I love it. One AA battery so it is not heavy. Slightly beveled sides (wider on the top) so it's easy to pick up if needed. Very comfortable in the hand and is symmetrical so it's great for left handers too. I called it a wireless mouse because it works with an included USB dongle or with your native Bluetooth. The dongle stores inside if not used. Easy to set up - follow the instructions because there is an option to link to Bluetooth or the dongle. You can switch between the two, indicated on the bottom. The power switch is good. I only turn it off when it's in my backpack. On the desk, it sleeps and wakes seemlessly. The optical sensor on the bottom works onall surfaces and there is no red laser to blind you when you look for the switch. You can adjust the dots per inch sensitivity for your needs. This helps me for drawing sketches with the mouse. There are buttons. The usual left, middle, and right. The middle button is a wide scroll wheel, and it works as left and tight tilt, too. Two thumb buttons (for right hand use). All buttons are configurable through the provided application. I'm not using them for anything yet, but it's a nice option.
All-in-all I highly recommend this inexpensive wireless mouse for every day use. I have an expensive Alienware wired gaming mouse specificly for gaming use. But for work documentation, occasional CAD use, surfing the web, this is my new favorite. Dell MS5120W.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
My system came pretty well cleaned. It had something oily on part of the top, but that wiped off, though some had gotten into the dust screen so that had to be removed to clean. There were no scratches on the system, and everything seems in good working order.

As most other reviews have mentioned, mine came with the Ryzen pro 5 2400g, which is a 65W part, vs. the 2400ge which is 35W TDP but lower clocked. The top is covered in mesh for better airflow, probably because the 2400g does get hot in this little machine. Running a stress test, I was able to get it up to 93C but the cooling system, in a room at 68F, was able to keep it there so it never throttled (which it should do if it gets to 95C) and maintained just under 3.6ghz on all 4 cores (the base clock). Stressing a single core, it will go up to 3.9ghz, so it could be that others who were having issues with performance might have some problem with their system.

It came with 8GB of SK hynix DDR4 2666mhz RAM and a 256GB (older) Samsung PCI-E SSD. I got the SATA drive cage as well, which does have a fan for both its drive and the PCI-E drive that sits under the fan. I actually had a 16GB DDR4 3200mhz RAM set not being used, so I put that in and the system sees it as 2933mhz, which is the maximum RAM frequency supported for this CPU without overclocking, which this system does not do. So, I'd recommend at least picking up a second stick to get the benefits of dual channel which is supported, but if you buy all new RAM, I'd recommend picking up the faster stuff as well as it'll handle it.

My system came with the HDMI module so it has 1 HDMI and 2 display ports. Accessories were a very generic USB wired keyboard, a very generic USB wired mouse, a mini USB wireless dongle and a mini USB bluetooth dongle. You can put a PCI-E wireless/bluetooth module in this system, so that might be a better option. Keep in mind that this system has antenna for the PCI-E wireless/bluetooth module, but does not come with the module, and you will most likely (I had to, someone else mentioned this as well) have to remove the motherboard to get to the antenna wires, as they seem to have been tucked underneath. To remove the motherboard, you have 4 screws plus the 3 that hold the heatsink onto the CPU. The problem here is that you shouldn't remove the heatsink without cleaning and reapplying thermal paste, so you basically will have to rebuild the system to install the wireless module properly.

The power adapter this comes with has been mentioned at least once before. Mine was not a HP OEM power brick, but a generic one. It had the right barrel connector, but it's a 90W 19V 4.7A adapter. It appears the OEM adapter should be a 19.5V 4.62A, but finding the OEM 90W adapter is tough unless you want to spend a lot. My system does immediately power on when plugged in as others have mentioned, but you can turn it off and it will stay off, and seems to run ok on the generic adapter.

One thing I think someone else mentioned, but the first generation Zen processors (Ryzen 1000 and 2000 series) are not on the Windows 11 supported CPU list, and you will be blocked from upgrading to Windows 11 on this machine. It does have TPM 2.0, so it's just the CPU that is blocking you. Microsoft does have instructions for getting around this, by entering a registry entry to tell the installer to allow unsupported CPUs, but Windows updates still will not let you upgrade directly. You'll need to download the installer/updater from Microsoft then run that. It does appear that upgrading from the installer works, though people were originally saying you would have to install fresh. Anyway, doing this, you have to agree that you are fine with possible issues and lack of driver support, so do it at your own risk I guess.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This HP 24mh monitor has a clear, crisp display and is the perfect size for desktop use (not too big, not too small). It accepts both HDMI and DisplayPort inputs (and even VGA for old school PCs). While Windows will select 60Hz refresh rate by default, you can go into Windows' display settings and select 75Hz refresh rate for this monitor. The 75Hz refresh rate really does help smooth out motion. You should also go into the monitor's "Image" menu setting and set Response Time to Level 3 which provides the best VSYNC performance. One of the best features that places this monitor above and beyond its price range is the 90-degree rotating screen, height adjustment, and swiveling base. The stand is rock-solid without any wobble. The speakers are just fine once you discover the menu control I explain below:

HOW TO FIX LOW VOLUME SOUND: The built-in speakers are better than some reviewers indicate. I believe most people don't discover that the monitor menu has its own volume control that's set to 50% volume by factory default. If you just connect this monitor to the PC you'll automatically get sound through the HP speakers via HDMI or DisplayPort (you only have to use the separate audio cable when using the VGA input). But no matter how high you turn up your PC volume control, you'll only get 50% volume from the monitor's speakers which is why people complain about low volume. To fix this, all you need to do is go to the "Management" tab of the monitor menu, select "Audio", and then turn up the volume control from 50 (default) to 100 and you'll find the monitor speakers are plenty loud. After that, you'll only have to use your PC volume control as normal.

This is a great quality monitor with features beyond its price range. Fantastic value, HP!

ADDITIONAL NOTE: HP sells an identical monitor to the HP 24mh under the model P24h. The only difference is that the P24h has a black plastic logo strip along the bottom instead of silver like the 24mh. Everything else is identical (specs, speakers, height adjustable stand, etc.) plus the P24h comes with both an HDMI cable and a DisplayPort cable.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This little computer is a bargain for a desktop system or an HTPC. It has plenty of compute power for an small office or home PC. It can even run some low end 3D games, although you might have to turn down the graphics settings in the games. All you need is a monitor along with a Display Port to HDMI cable for a complete setup. You can download OpenOffice or LibreOffice for an effective office software suite. It is one of the most inexpensive ways that you can get a Windows 11 compatible computer.

Any time you buy one of these refurbished systems, and i have bought a few, you can expect some minor variations in configuration from what is stated. They usually give you more rather than less (which would annoy buyers). Mine came as advertised with the one exception that it has a 3400G processor that is a bit faster than the 3400GE, but that draws 65W of power instead of 35W. I would have preferred the lower wattage GE for my application, but it is fine. Internally, it came with a Toshiba 256GB M.2 NVMe SSD, an Intel AX210 M.2 WiFI/BT card, and a single Micron Technology 8GB DDR4 2666 SODIMM memory card.

It has a empty removable tray for a 2.5" SATA HD or SSD. You have to remove that tray to get to the M.2 slots underneath. It is a bit harder to remove that tray than it is on the 800 G2 or 805 G5 that I also own. it is only more difficult because there are cables both front and back on it. The back is the SATA ribbon cable and the front is the fan cable. I think the safest way to remove it is to first remove the SATA connector from the tray carefully so that you don't pull the ribbon cable out of its connector on the board - which wouldn't be the end of the world, but they are obnoxious to reinsert. Then you pull off the front screw. slide the tray forward, lift it up and out, then rotate it towards the front to not pull out the fan connector. BTW, mine came with the SATA ribbon cable already pulled out of the board - perhaps the only minor complaint I had.

Because there is no HDD in the tray, you do not get the special bushings it takes to mount a drive there. But, I found that drone M3 anti-vibration standoffs, such as the ones from FPVDrone, work well enough. You can find them here on Amazon.

If you hold down ESC when you boot it, it goes into the BIOS. In that BIOS are diagnostics to run that you can use to check out your computer. I recommend that you do so before installing the OS. Mine passed just fine. You also might want to go through the settings. I couldn't get mine to boot from a USB stick until I checked the box in the BIOS to allow that. Businesses often lock down USB ports for security reasons, and these PCs come out of businesses that have moved on to more current computers.

If you are looking for a low cost way to get a computer for non-gaming usage, this is a great value.

text:
I was searching for a Plex Media server upgrade to my aging and stuck-on-Windows-10 HP EliteBook, and my reseach brought me to this listing. This is the first time I've ever bought a PC refurbished, and also my first experience with SFF PCs like this one originally designed for business/commercial use (all my other PCs were consumer oriented). As with most refurbished products, you never really know what will happen and you just gotta trust that the company did their due diligence with it before selling it to you.

UNBOXING: Out of the box, the packaging is very generous and was basically more than enough to pad all the crucial components. It came in the super thick bubble wrap that made it impossible to rattle around in the box. The mouse and keyboard came in a separated box, and other accessories were in separate bags.

CONDITION: I don't know if I got lucky or maybe this company really does refurb items properly, but my unit was pretty much immaculate inside and out. No visible scratches or scuffs on the outside, and the inside was shockingly dust-free. The ports all looked perfect (usually they would get mangled or scuffed up from constant use), and the AC power adapter was equally as immaculate. Either way, I'm more than satisfied

BOOTING UP: Setting it up was was dead simple. Turning it on brings you to the "HP Secure Boot" screen and you load straight into the Windows 11 setup screen. It was definitely a good taste of the performance of this PC because it just blazed through the setup screens.

IN USE: The clean Windows 11 installation was definitely true, because there was basically ZERO bloatware pre-installed. After all the updates that it installed shortly after setup, getting everything up and ready for my Plex server use was incredibly fast and simple. The i5-8500T (which I specifically looked for in my research since this gen of CPU had the improved Intel Quick Sync), 16GB of RAM and the 256GB SSD are such a big step up.

Even after opening up various Chrome tabs, NAS software, and transcoding my media library fails to cause this system to slow down or run into any performance issue. The fan does spool up and the PC gets a bit warm, but unless you have this PC right near your face or you have it placed on your hands, you won't really notice it running.

ACCESSORIES: they were generous to include the mouse and keyboard, WIFI + BT dongle, and DisplayPort dongle in the package. While they all worked pretty well, I only ended up using the DisplayPort dongle and the WIFI + BT dongle ONLY for the BT. My own mouse and keyboard were better, and Ethernet will ALWAYS trump WIFI especially for Plex use.

The WIFI + BT is half-hit half-miss. The BT part works pretty well with no disconnects experienced, but the Realtek chip for WIFI using the archaic 802.11n standard; my Wifi speeds were limited to 140-160mpbs up/down For comparison, my gigabit Ethernet basically hit 980mpbs up/down. If you have an Ethernet connection available, I STRONGLY suggest you use it with this PC.

VERDICT: This PC and, by extension, this refurb company have definitely set the bar high because I am very happy with this PC. While long terms reliable is still up in the air, the fact that this SFF PC with an 8th gen CPU was basically in immaculate condition and runs like a $1000+ machine is impressive. I'll update my review if I run into any issues down the line, but for now, solid 10/10

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Needed to replace a PC that would not accept Win11 (thanks MS 😤). Has VESA mount sockets, so a cheap TV wall mount put it on the wall behind my desk and cleared some needed desktop real estate.
Brass tacks: This is NOT intended to be a gaming PC. It is at its best being used for personal or business web work, word processing, spreadsheets, email, light video/audio/picture editing, and simple gaming. It boots fast, runs fast, and is relatively quiet. All those complaining about fan noise must realize this uses a desktop-type socket insert processor, so it runs hotter and has higher cooling needs. In practice, it is no noisier than the little USB fan you have on your desk.
For the nerds who love to tinker with PCs, this thing is really cool! One thumbscrew opens it up. SSD, memory, processor, eMMC slots are all swappable. There is even an accessory port that can be swapped between VGA, USB, HDMI, even Serial Port!
All of this in a package the size of a DVD player. (Remember those?🤣)
It arrived very well packaged and cosmetically, I haven't found a single scratch or wear mark. The only thing missing was that "New PC" smell 🤣.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
Got this to use as a Streaming Box so that I could avoid using the poorly written apps that came installed on my Smart TV. And since it was not new, it came with some scuffs and minor cosmetic damage on the outside, but otherwise it was just fine with its performance. And for the price, it was a great deal considering this cost more than triple when new!

What I liked:
Small! Very easy to open for upgrades. May be a bit confusing if you don't know what you are doing, so HP proves a full step-by-step video on YouTube that shows you how to change everything inside. Consumes around 70 Watts of power. Supports 1x 2.5 SSD and 2x NVME drives at the same time. Comes with 2 Display Ports so if you plan to use this with HDMI, you will need an adapter or the HDMI Option card module. 1x USB 3.1 Gen 2 and 1x USB 3.1 Gen 1 on front with support for 1.5A charging. 1x USB 3.1 Gen 2 Type C in front with support for 5V 3A charging. 4x USB 3.1 in rear. Front headphone and mic jacks. 1x ethernet jack in rear.
Upgradable 8th Gen Intel CPU. (mine came with a i5 8500T) Hardware supports Windows 10/11, Supports 2x DDR4 2666 SODIMM (32G Max) M2 Slot to upgrade WiFi/BlueTooth to latest standards. Refurbisher did a great job in cleaning the dust and dirt out of the fans and heatsinks! No dust was seen anywhere inside my unit.

A configurable option card slot in rear for a single output upgrade choice of:
DisplayPort™ 1.2,
HDMI™ 2.0,
VGA,
USB Type-C™ with alt mode display,
USB Type-C™ with Power Delivery,
Discrete Graphics Option Card with DisplayPort™ 1.4,
Thunderbolt 3.0, Serial Port,
Fiber NIC
Serial Port.

What I disliked:
Intel UHD Graphics 630 means you will not be playing any AAA titles on this thing. Lite gaming is possible but that's it. But I did not get it to game so it's not really a problem for me. No HDMI without module (mine game with a Serial module)
Note online sites say that modules may not work due to the security on these mini PC's that for some reason can't be easily circumvented by consumers. I have not experienced this yet but I will update if the issue arises.
Due to the 6 core 8th gen CPU, Windows 11 doesn't run smoothly on this device. So to get better performance, I had to install Windows 10 on it. Might work better with a i7 CPU upgrade. Mine was missing the NVMe standoffs and screws. You will have to buy these online if you plan to upgrade from SSD to NVMe.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I bought this months ago, but amazon showed it in my history and I had not written a review for a product(s) I like and use daily. But as a 30 year IT person, I often have needs to find cheap PCs either for clients or myself at home.

Earlier this year I was in the market for a miniPC, as I wanted to use it as a server for my home network (running linux). Its me, so I didn't want to spend a ton of money, but wanted something decent, that I could upgrade. I'm familiar with this product line, as these are business grade computers, so I've used this specific model at companies (when these were new). In short, HP G-series PCs are pretty reliable, and last longer than their home ones. So no surprise they are for sale as refurbished on here.

I was comparing a Dell of similar spec to this one, but this one just won out for price point for what I was getting. I liked them so much, I bought two of them. One for the server, and one to use as spare testing Windows machine that didn't take up a ton of space (and wasn't a laptop).

Full Disclosure, I added a 500GB SSD NVMe M.2 drive as the boot drive, so your results may vary in terms of speed. But I will say, it was speedy with the stock drive that came with it (see below)

Here's what I liked..

- First off, who it came from. I was pleasantly surprised that the Amazon Certified Reseller that this came from (as the box said) is a company I know from my IT experience for decades. While they are a business2business company, many HP (and Dell) PCs I bought over the years, came from this company. So I know they know what they are doing. However, I can't say yours will come from this place, but have hopes that others are as high calibre as this one since they would be Amazon-certified also.

- This thing is small, its no bigger than a standard mouse pad.
- It's very clean, it almost looked new. No dents, scratches, or dings. The inside was spotless and the CPU had been remounted with fresh paste!
- Its powerful. I've done some hard video encoding and testing, and it just purrs along, and this was still with the included 500GB drive!
- It's quiet, unless I'm chewing the processor up with something the fans spin up. But even then it is not as loud as my desktop workstation (an HP also!).
- It's an energy sipper. I connected a power meter to it for a month, it used so little power (vs my desktop)
- Processor speed is pretty speedy and windows preinstall is pretty zippy on it
- This model has 16GB of ram which is plenty of ram these days for most applications
- Two drive support. This can take 2 drives, a 2.5" SATA drive & a NVMe M.2 2280 drive (just add a screw!)
- Plenty of USB 3.0 , 2 USB Type A (flat plug) and 1 USB-C in the front and 4 USB Type A ports in the back
- 2 Displayport ports for dual monitor support and a VGA port
- Onboard 10/100 ethernet & audio
- This specific renewed model comes with a Windows 10 Pro license! (some do not!)
- If you're security minded, this does come with TMP 1.0 and other UEFI related security tools.
- Since this is an HP Business PC, spare parts and support are easy to find and locate. Everything is HP standard, well tested, and made for years of reliability.

Here's what I thought was "meh"

- Because its tiny, the power supply is a brick on a cord. Not a big deal and the cord from the brick to the PC is long, but the brick itself has to be put somewhere vs a straight cord.
- This model does not come with WiFi or the antenna kit. The MiniPCIe slot exists though so Wifi can be added later and it's not a show stopper for me as these will be hard wired.

Here's what I didn't like..

None. I do not have any huge things I do not like about this product, other than my meh. I'm extremely pleased with this product!

Overall, as stated above, I'm extremely pleased with this product. Add a NVMe M.2 drive as your boot drive and you will be screaming for a low low price.

title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I ordered two of these. They were advertised as being refurbished by a certified refurbisher. These were going to be put in use as a continuous operation thin client, so i decided to double check the condition of the internals. I opened the case and on both units, the hard drive was installed incorrectly, and both were missing hard drive mount grommets. I pulled the heat sinks off the processors to check thermal paste. on the first, only 75% of the processor had contact with the heat sink from thermal paste, and the silicon thermal pads were falling apart and missing in some places. On the second unit, it appeared that thermal paste was applied by a stencil, however only about 50% of the processor was making contact because the heat sink was installed incorrectly, and the mounting screws were cross threaded into the chassis. This unit also had degraded silicon pads. I corrected the issues myself and put these in service. They are functioning well. Had this been left as provided, hot spots on the processors would have significantly impacted performance and shortened the life of the processors.

I did reach out to the seller and was offered a return authorization. I let them know that I corrected the issue, and it was pretty much left at that. I guess I expected something to cover my efforts to correct their failed attempt at refurbishing. I did ask if thermal management was something they addressed in their refurbishment process and did not get an answer on that. Being that I ordered 2, and both were in poor condition, I suspect this is the level of quality that can be expected.

I realize these are older units, and I would fully expect this quality from a private seller or surplus purchase, but I specifically ordered refurbished units to ensure they would serve the purpose I needed. I still think I got a good deal with this purchase, but understand, you will need some level of technical capabilities to ensure these meet the needs you have. Always check, because the issues above would quickly render these paperweights. Had these failed due to me not checking, the rating would have been 1 star, but because i was able to catch this ahead of failure, I saved the seller 2 stars on this review.

text:
I know that refurbished electronics are a bit of a gamble. Even if the people who do the cleaning and refit have checked all the boxes, who knows what abuses the machine suffered in its former life. All that said, my expectations were well tempered. Yours should be too! This is used merchandise, so be prepared to contact customer service if something isn’t right, and don’t make a fuss unless they fail to make it right. If that doesn’t sound like fun to you, then buy a new machine.

In my case, the computer I received was immaculate inside and out. I suspect it had pretty low hours before it was refurbished. It boots quickly and runs almost silent (you won’t hear it unless there’s nothing else in the room that makes a sound). No issues with the fresh windows install (don’t throw out the papers in the box! You’ll need them to get started). Unlike many of the refurb PC’s in this price range, this has actual, built-in wifi instead of one of those useless USB dongles. The included usb keyboard and mouse were HP branded and appeared to be new. A lot of reviews on other machines complain about super-cheap generic peripherals, so this was a nice surprise. There was also a display port to hdmi converter included, so you’d only need a standard hdmi cable to connect. I opted to buy a display to hdmi cable instead, so I didn’t end up using it.

It’s not a new computer, and it’s definitely not a gaming PC (I’m using it as a light duty steam machine, but not running anything with high processing or graphics demand), but it’s exactly the product that was described. Mine was perfect out of the box, but if it wasn’t, I’m confident the seller would have made it right!

Was a little dusty inside. Had one 16 GB stick of RAM Samsung brand. Looks like there was a WiFi card at one point, which was removed. Appears that the rear antenna external part was removed and the wire was cut, leaving a cut piece of wire laying around under the motherboard. The front side antenna was left there. Value for money was good. Detailed post below.

Everything as described in the description was provided and nothing was missing. The model I purchased did not include WiFi and Bluetooth (which I knew), but I did purchase a WiFi card and a set of antennas separate to install myself. They did include a USB WiFi dongle, which was not the best performing one, but it worked. Also included was a mouse and keyboard set, a DC adapter, and a separate power cable.

Before I did anything to this machine, I did make sure it booted and it booted up just fine and Windows 10 Pro was installed and activated. So no issues with booting up. No bloatware or anything as well which was great. After powering off, and inspecting the back, I noticed in one of the holes there was a cut wire nearly sticking out the hole and I had no idea what it was. I tried to pull it out thinking it was just a small piece of wire but couldn't. More on this later on.

When I took this apart, there was a noticeable bit of dust inside which I just cleaned with some compressed air. The CPU cooler fan was clean though as well as the heat sink. There was single 16 GB stick of RAM that I later changed to two identical 8 GB sticks. The thermal paste was still new and good, but I replaced it anyways before putting this back together.

Now the interesting part, there were antennas already installed so it looks like there may have been a WiFi card at some point. The wire going to the front was still intact, but the wire going to the back appears to have been cut. On this machine, the rear antenna has a little piece that protrudes the rear side about 1/4 an inch out and snaps on to the back. It looks like that someone removed that external piece and instead of removing the whole antenna, they simply cut the wire connecting to that piece. This resulted in a piece of cut wire just laying around under the motherboard which in my opinion is very sloppy and some additional care could have gone to proper removal of this. I also don't like having lose wires hanging around inside machines since they may cause damage if they come into contact with any conductive parts. I attached an image showing the cut wire. May not be on the seller, but I think as a refurbished machine seller some time should go into inspecting the machines for things like this (especially since that cut wire was one of the first things I noticed before even taking it apart). Anyways, the antennas were replaced and a new card installed and connected.

After putting it all back together, restarted the machine and the WiFi is significantly better. Other than that, everything else worked great as they did before I took the machine apart.

After my old inkjet finally gave up the ghost (and after spending way too much on replacement cartridges over the years), I decided to make the jump to laser. Did a bunch of research and landed on this HP Color Laserjet Pro - honestly, wish I'd made the switch sooner.
Setup was pretty straightforward, though the wireless connection took a couple tries to get right. Nothing too frustrating, just had to restart my router once. The HP Smart app walked me through most of it. Once it was connected, printing from my laptop and phone has been seamless.
The print quality is really impressive - colors are vibrant without being oversaturated, and text is crisp. I mainly use it for client presentations and occasional family photos, and both look great. The speed is a huge upgrade from my old printer too. What used to take forever now prints in seconds.
Scanner works well for documents, though the photo scanning is just okay - not amazing but gets the job done for basic stuff. Copy function is handy for quick duplicates without having to mess with my computer.
Only minor complaints: it's definitely bigger than my old printer, so make sure you have the desk space. Also runs a bit warm when printing a lot of pages, but that seems normal for laser printers. The toner cartridges aren't cheap, but they last way longer than inkjet cartridges did.
Overall really happy with this purchase. It's been reliable for about 6 months now with zero paper jams or connection issues. Would definitely recommend if you're looking for a dependable color laser for home office use.

title: 1.0 out of 5 stars
text:
The reality is, if you use this printer for homeschooling (or you just print things fairly often), you're going to need a rich husband (or a rich wife, I don't discriminate 😉).

I didn't try to print entire books or anything, just a few pages every day or so for normal homework assignments. I also tried printing out a couple pictures, but nothing major. It took 3 months for the printer to say that all 4 cartridges were "beyond low".

Buying the real HP cartridges costs ~$400 for all 4. Those cartridges are good for about 1200 pages.

Or...go buy an EcoTank 4950 and get 7500+ pages and it costs less than $100 to replace all 4 colors of ink. It literally costs less to buy a nice EcoTank printer than it does to replace the toner in this HP printer. 😔🤦‍♂️

But, since it took 3 months, we're past the return window. I'm out almost $600 on a printer that I can't afford to use. HP, if you're reading this, please let me return this!

Aside from the toner, the printer works great. My only complaint was that it was really hard to scan one page in a book because the LCD screen doesn't fold out of the way. So, where the book would normally just hang out of the scanner while you scanned one page, there wasn't really room for that. Definitely a design flaw.

P.S. If you're thinking "I'll just go buy off-brand toner and save a ton of money; no big deal", then think again! HP has specifically put chips in their OEM cartridges to prevent this, and you'll have to disable all firmware updates, wait for the latest "fake" cartridges to come out, then buy that (with firmware updates off forever) to use an off-brand. It's a pain, and the quality of the off-brand cartridges isn't great anyway. You end up with weirdness in your prints pretty frequently.

All in all, this isn't a printer for the average or even above average family. It's clearly aimed at milking businesses for toner fees over time. Just buy an EcoTank. You have been warned.

title: 1.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This printer might seem like a good deal at first, but it’s really just a ploy to lock you into buying expensive ink from HP.

I bought this to replace my HP 4255e after its printhead failed, and even the replacement head didn’t work. This printer cost me about $50 less than that replacement head alone, so I thought I was getting a bargain.

The setup was straightforward, and it connected to my network without any issues. However, I’m uneasy about how HP connects to the printer over the internet—who knows what data they’re collecting?

One glaring flaw is the lack of automatic two-sided printing. Instead, you have to manually reload the paper to print on the other side, following on-screen prompts. It’s an annoying step back from the fully automated feature I had before.

The switch to a single color cartridge is a step backward, too. It’s more convenient, but with separate cartridges, you could at least use up each color fully before replacing it. Now, you’re throwing money away when one color runs out.

The so-called “free” 6-month trial of HP’s Instant Ink (Dynamic Security chip on printer ink ) program is just a sneaky way to milk more money out of you. It’s not really an ink subscription; it’s a deal where you pay for the number of pages you print each month, regardless of how much ink you actually use. Even if you print just one word on a page, it counts towards your limit. If you cancel the program, any ink they’ve already sent becomes useless, forcing you to buy their overpriced cartridges. I canceled it and switched to aftermarket ink, which works just as well for half the price.

Print quality is also a letdown. It’s nowhere near the standard of my old 8610, though it’s adequate for basic home printing. Forget about using it for anything professional or for printing barcodes—scan codes often don’t work on the first try. title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
This thing was pretty easy to set up. I'm not big on using a smart phone for setting up computer peripherals so I ignored that part in the Setup Guide. Since I planned to connect my printer with a USB cable, I just skipped ahead in the Setup Guide to the Manual Installation instructions. The first step is filling the ink tanks which is pretty simple and takes only a few minutes - make sure you follow the directions. Then came the first hiccup - you have to install 2 printheads onto the print carriage. The tiny picture in the book wasn't much help in figuring out how to put the printheads in place. But take a breath and just examine the things for a minute and you'll figure out how to snap them into place (they only go in one way and the printhead cover won't close unless they are correctly installed).

If, like me, you are using a USB cable to connect the printer, I'm not sure why you have to download and install the "HP Smart Software". But I did as instructed and followed the instructions which weren't much more than "plug in the USB cable" and you are ready to go.

Then hiccup #2: for my first print job, I attempted to print a picture from the Windows Photo app. Click on "Print" and nothing. Oh No! But then I noticed a error message at the bottom of the print dialog - something about a conflict with another device. I then turned OFF the switch labelled "Let the app change my printing preferences" and voila! The printer sprang to life and printed my picture. And no problems since. This could have easily been a Windows issue having nothing to do with the printer, but I mention it just in case it happens to someone else.

HUZZAH! 1. Simple setup for USB connection. 2. color prints look very nice (see my Caveats below) 3. small physical footprint for an All in One - respectful of the limited real estate on your computer desk 4. Fairly zippy print speed 5. Two sided printing works fine 6. I really like the automatic "Sleep Mode". You don't have to worry about turning off the printer when you are done with your job. And it will instantly awaken when you need to print something. I just leave the printer ON 24/7 and let it sleep away when I'm not using it. 7. This model has an ID Card copying feature. It will copy both sides of an ID card and print both sides to the same sheet of paper. I haven't tried this, but the feature looks useful (you will have to download the 104 page User Guide from the HP web site to see how this function works). 8. This printer will print envelopes but, again, you will need to refer to the 104 page User Guide to see how to load the envelopes.

GRUMBLE: 1. Buttons on the Control Panel are not well marked and difficult to see - get out your label maker! 2. print head installation a little tricky 3. Copy function (including the auto feeder) works well but copying is a little pokey.

These petty grumbles will not let me waiver from my 5 star review.

A couple of caveats about my review: 1. As I set my printer up with a USB connection, I didn't attempt to set up, or even mess with, the WiFi mode. 2. I've never used an Ink Tank printer before so I can't comment on that function. But filling the tanks was quick and simple. A couple of other reviews had complaints of spilled ink, but the supplied ink bottles appeared pretty spill proof to me. Even turning them upside down to fill the tanks didn't result in a single spilled drop. 3. The few color prints I have made are documents and cartoons I printed on plain paper. I have not attempted to print any photo quality prints on photo paper so I can't comment on the print quality of photos. 5. I have no need for the SCAN function, so I've never tried it.

Finally, you will benefit from downloading the comprehensive 104 page User Guide from the HP Support web site. It's in PDF format so you can read it from Adobe Acrobat Reader.

text: I purchased this printer in June 2020 for the scanning and printing ability as well as the compact size. I didn't need the portability, but thought that would be an added bonus just in case. The printer worked fine for approximately 3.5 years, although it did seem to go through ink rather quickly considering I don't print very much. I mostly used for scanning documents which worked fine. However, there is apparently a Lithium Ion battery in this printer required for power, despite the fact that the printer has an AC adapter plug. I have never used this printer for travel and it has always remained plugged into an AC outlet, but after 3.5 years the battery (that I didn't even know existed until now) has died and the printer shut off without warning, explanation, or error code. After entirely too much research through the completely unhelpful HP website, I finally just googled the battery SN and discovered you can purchase replacement batteries for $106. I purchased a battery, received a damaged box with no instructions other than to put the battery into the printer. I did so and the printer has been showing an error code for 3 days stating "Faulty Battery - The battery is faulty and must be replaced. For ordering information, visit the HP Support website." I tried searching the HP Support website again for help, but there is no information anywhere about replacing these batteries. When I search for the printer on support, it directs me to order a support plan with a monthly fee in order to receive help from support. I've now requested a replacement battery, but I'm not hopeful at finding a solution at this point. After all of this, I would say that unless you have unlimited funds and don't mind replacing the battery every three years, I would not recommend this printer. I also wouldn't spend over $400 for a printer again that also requires a non-rechargeable battery for use. I'll be looking for a cheaper printer that's easier to replace next. Preferably not HP.

title: 3.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I use this monitor as I work from home 4 days out of the week & I absolutely loved it at first but the more I used it I learned that it simply doesn’t live up to the price point. Before I dive into the cons some of the pros are that for its size it’s honestly not that heavy, it’s pretty clunky but I had no issues carrying it around by myself. The monitor slides up and down which is awesome so you can be sure whether or not your webcam is on & it’s like an added layer of privacy (the webcam is super high up so if you’re short like me your head might get cut off).

And last PRO - The monitor also comes with built in speakers, they get pretty loud & although my MacBook Air sound much better the fact this monitor even comes with speakers & a built in microphone is pretty dope! some of the expensive gaming monitors don’t even come with speakers!

Ok, now for the cons…
1. If you are saving up for a high quality, expensive monitor to last you a long while please keep your options open. If you have expendable income & this isn’t a big purchase for you then buy it but if this is possibly a big purchase I honestly wouldn’t take the chance. I was able to buy this with a work from home stipend & while I make a decent salary I would be extremely upset if I paid for this with my hard earned money.

2. I had high expectations for the picture and color quality but those expectations weren’t met, I was actually a little shocked at how bland and fuzzy the screen appears. The colors seem washed out, the best way I can think to describe it is being kind of matte and not “glossy”, the picture isn’t crispy. Even just browning the web if you look close to the screen you can see the text looks slightly fuzzy. This isn’t a big deal but again, it should be clear and crispy for $500.

3. The size is awesome for gaming, if you have a Gaming PC with a graphics card this would honestly do the job but my Truly honest opinion is if you are interested in buying this for strictly gaming I’m not sure if this will be enjoyable to truly enjoy the gaming experience. I would look for monitors specifically built for gamers.

4. IT BREAKS VERY EASILY!!!! I initially thought it was a tough monitor as I’ve taken it out of town with me, hauling it in and out of the car without issue, while it held up great in the car it didn’t stand a chance against a small light piece of plastic. A figurine I keep near my desk somehow fell against the monitor & it completely demolished the screen. Immediatley broke the screen with a 2-3inch wide black line down the screen with the right side glitching out. It gradually got worse over the next few days, at first the left hand side still worked great so I honestly didn’t mind since the screen is so incredibly large but eventually horizontal purple & green lines started popping up making it hard to read my work files.

I understand that if something it’s a monitor screen it will break but I truly was shocked at how sensitive this monitor was to barely being hit by the plastic figurine. Growing up my mom was in IT and worked on computers for a school district and my uncle built gaming PC’s so I’ve used a lot of different computer monitors both high quality and crappy - unfortunately this monitor is up there with the crappy quality ones due to the fact the entire screen went out so easily.

I truly expected higher quality and for the monitor itself to be quite durable since it’s over $500.. I’ve had run of the mill monitors that have fallen off the back of a truck & still worked perfect. Since it’s a curved monitor I’m sure that plays a part into the screen being so sensitive.

The monitor lasted roughly 6 months with no issues but I really enjoyed using it as a work monitor & I felt spoiled due to how big the monitor is. I honestly think it’s BIGGER than 32 inches, it feels more like 35-38 inches because my 27inch monitor at the office is half its size.

Like all the refurbished stuff, what I get from "supplier A" may not be what you get from "supplier B". That's just how this works. If you go over to the little pull down, you can see a number of folks who all are happy to sell you one of these.

What I happened to get this time was: No SSD bracket, and no DVD. I did get a keyboard, mouse, power cord, built in WiFi, the specified RAM and NVME drive. There is "another place" you can go and get them pretty darn cheap ....

Everything functions as it should. It booted fine to Windows 10. That went away as soon as I had a chance to fiddle the BIOS and load Linux.

Mine happened to come with two 8 GB RAM sticks to make up the 16 GB needed. Might another one come with four 4GB? I have no idea. The "two stick" option makes adding more RAM a bit easier. Oddly enough the BIOS showed the installed ram running as 2666MHz rather than 2400MHz. I guess I got lucky. The NVME in mine is a stock Lenovo part. Is it new or has it lived there forever? There's no way to tell. BIOS was last updated in 2024.

Mechanically everything looks fine. No major scratches or dents. Nothing busted or caved in. It would look fine if you wanted to put it on a desktop. This is not a super duper modern CPU and 16 GB is not a lot of RAM. That will impact how it will do running Windows vs something a bit newer.

For the price, I'm quite happy with what I got. Right now this one is the "low cost leader" of the M920s refurbs. That's true here on Amazon and on "that other place".

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
[This review is for a refurbished M720S 16GB / 512GB SSD]

Measured at about 3.5" x 10.5" x 13.5" the M720S is a nice little compact desktop. It is sturdy built and Includes 8 USB ports, microphone and headset port, and 2 DVI (display ports). Of course the downside of such size is the limited ability of upgrades, however the M720S can easily host an extra drive and 3 extra PCI cards (including a graphic card) as long as they are low profile (2.5" high). The one I got also has a laptop style DVD drive. I would give this computer 4/5 due to limited overall performance.

Now if you decided to buy this machine the 2nd question is, should I buy it here on Amazon? And here it is questionable. The machine is refurbished, you don't get to see the actual machine you will be getting, so they make you feel like you will get a like-new machine, but mine had some scratches on it and the packaging was very minimal and it sat in Styrofoam which broke and pieces of it were embedded in the computer grill and had to be manually cleaned. There was not even a "fragile" or a "this side up" sticker on the box. I can see how this can easily be a DOA due to shipping.

Moreover, the packaging was missing the DVI to HDMI plug which makes it impossible to connect to any modern screen. I had to contact Amazon to get a replacement and they sent me a new cable for free. I decided to buy from Amazon, which is more expensive than other outlets, because I thought it would be hassle-free and the box will be new, however it was not the case.

Remember that this machine can be found in many different configurations, as far as CPU architecture and speed, memory size, and drive size. It looks the same from the outside, but you are paying for what's inside. In any event never get a machine that cannot be upgraded to Win 11, that would substantially limit the lifetime on it.

A word about software- the machine comes with a brand new Win 11 install, it has no issue and does not come with any bloatware or adware that I could see. The WiFi / BT plugin works well. If you intend to use this machine for gaming, be prepared to add a $100 graphics card to make this machine viable for gaming, otherwise it is a nice home-office machine.

Summary:
Pros:
1. Nice form factor
2. Relatively cheap i7 CPU
3. Win 11 software / no bloatware
4. Reliable manufacturer / return policy
5. DVD drive, lots of SSD space
6. Easy to upgrade

Cons:
1. It is not 'like new' shape
2. Bad packaging - missing add-ons
3. On-board GPU is not good enough for gaming and has DVI out only
4. Needs plug for WiFi / BT (supplied as extra in box)

Overall 3.5 / 5, I rounded it up to 4 since at the end I am happy with the purchase, but really the packaging here should be better. Hope this was helpful for you to make a decision.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I am incredibly impressed with the sheer multitasking power packed into this compact chassis. The AMD Ryzen V2748 processor is a total workhorse, featuring 8 cores and 16 threads that handle heavy workloads, massive Excel spreadsheets, and 4K video streaming simultaneously without any stuttering. Unlike many other mini PCs that struggle with heat, the thermal management here is top-notch; even under a heavy load, the fan remains a low, unobtrusive hum, and the unit stays remarkably cool to the touch. It comes pre-installed with a clean version of Windows 11 Pro and the 16GB of DDR4 RAM provides a very snappy user experience right out of the box, making it a perfect primary desktop replacement for anyone looking to reclaim their desk space.

The connectivity and upgrade potential are where this machine truly shines as a long-term investment. Having the ability to run a triple 4K monitor setup via the HDMI, DisplayPort, and full-featured Type-C ports is a game changer for productivity and creative work. I also appreciate that the internal layout is accessible, allowing for future RAM upgrades up to 64GB or swapping in a larger SSD if the 512GB NVMe drive eventually fills up. The build quality feels premium with a sleek, textured finish that doesn’t attract fingerprints, and the inclusion of a VESA mount allowed me to hide the entire PC behind my monitor for a completely wire-free look. For the price point, the performance-to-value ratio is simply unbeatable for a home office or a high-end media center.

Edit- After some tinkering, I came to the conclusion that the stock Sata SSD is too slow. I added an 500GB NVME for extra storage. This definitely helped the write speeds. I also ditched the Realtek RTL8852BE wifi card, and replaced it with an Intel Ax210. My wifi speeds DOUBLED, I went from 231mbps to 461mbps. My Bluetooth went from 5.3 to 5.4, a nice bonus. I added another 16gb of DDR4, to 32GB total. This is now a proper speed demon, capable of heavy multitasking. Don't get me wrong It was pretty good out of the box, BUT NOW IT'S GREAT!!!

Something to be aware of with these random brand mini PC's is that they can contain spyware. I did not know this until I watched a guys youtube video about how he got his AK1PLUS and it did not ask for microsoft sign in upon setting up the PC. Then he noticed chrome was pre installed and it had some sort of "up search" attached to it. Apparently the company that makes these PC's was sourcing out a 3rd party to put the operating systems on these mini PC's and I guess that 3rd party was adding stuff that was not approved by the manufacturer.
His solution was to reload windows on the PC.
This was 1 year ago and the issue seems to be resolved now as my AK1PLUS did not have this issue.
But regardless its something EVEYBODY should be aware of when purchasing these off brand mini PC's.
One last thing the included manual is about 99% useless.
Overall I give it 3 stars. I probably will NOT be buying any more of these.

text:
This is my third Chromebook and quite possibly my favorite. I came from an Asus C302, which, while great at the time was becoming long in the tooth with battery life and the touch screen responsiveness.

This is my first Lenovo and I have to say, it's fantastic. I knew what I was getting into with a Chromebook, but I really was surprised by the quality of this Chromebook, even after all the reviews.

The color - wow. It has to be seen in person and I LOVE the fact that the keyboard area mimics the outer shell. A very subtle and deep blue hue.

The keyboard looks and feels great. Very crisp and responsive, exceeding the feel and quality of laptops that cost four times as much. I don't really ever hear the fans except for a very quiet environment, and the heat seems about on par with what I've seen from previous laptops. That is to say - the fan kicks on sometimes and then it turns off. No big deal.

The weight is definitely something I had to adjust to, but in a good way. I feel like the weight is just about perfect although it could be a smidge lighter. It makes the unit feel of high quality rather than just cheap junk on the other hand.

The upward firing speakers are also a welcome change as my previous Chromebook had side firing speakers. The sound quality is quite decent, and surprised me even though the bass is a bit lacking. There is fidelity that is gained just by having upward firing speakers that can't be understated.

My only gripes would be that the display could stand to go a bit brighter for outdoor use, and near the track pad when I push the computer to move it slightly with my thumb into position, I can feel & hear a creak or a flex of some sort. Also at times the drag on the track pad is a bit much depending on the oil levels of your fingers.

Overall, a fantastic computer for the price - (I paid $299) and I would absolutely purchase again. I love the fact that the OS will be updated thru 2029. As with all Chromebooks, finding that harmony between hardware and ChromeOS updates is sometimes hard to find if you don't do your homework.

Cheers.

Affordable Workhorse Mouse That Just Works

The Lenovo 300 USB Wired Mouse is one of those products that proves you don’t need to spend much to get something dependable. At just a few dollars, this little mouse has been a surprisingly durable and reliable option for me over the years. It’s full-sized, which makes it more comfortable than the tiny travel mice, and the ambidextrous shape means it works equally well for left- or right-handed users.

Setup is as simple as it gets—plug it into a USB port and you’re good to go. No drivers, no fuss. The 1600 DPI optical sensor is accurate enough for everyday use, whether browsing, working on documents, or even some light gaming. The clicks feel crisp and responsive, and the scroll wheel has just the right amount of resistance.

There are a couple of things to keep in mind. It’s very lightweight, so if you prefer a mouse with heft, this might feel too airy. Also, it’s a basic three-button design—no side buttons, no customization, no extras. That said, it’s exactly what you’d expect from a budget office mouse: simple, reliable, and durable.

Bottom line: If you need a no-nonsense wired mouse for work, school, or as a backup, the Lenovo 300 is a fantastic bargain that consistently delivers.

title: 4.0 out of 5 stars
text:
I recently purchased a new computer monitor that has an audio output jack on it. This allows me to switch between my computer using the Display Port connection and my other devices that use HDMI without having to switch between different speakers (because any sound signal coming into the monitor is sent out the audio output jack). Because of this I was looking for a set of small speakers that could sit under the monitor but yet didn't require a separate power cable to clutter things up more.

I found some speakers that seemed to be what I was looking for, but then I realized that they didn't have a separate volume control. A separate volume control is crucial for my use because even though my computers allow volume adjustment within the operating system a standard HDMI device (such as a cable box, game system, etc.) does not and I needed a way to control the volume for those devices as well.

These speakers fit the bill! They are fairly small (although they don't fit completely under the monitor they are still fine for my purposes even when they are slightly blocked, see picture), they sound great, and best of all they just plug into a powered USB port on the back of the monitor to get their power - no cumbersome AC adapter and wiring!

Installation is super easy. Just setup the right speaker and connect the USB port to any powered USB port on your monitor or computer, plug the standard audio cable into the audio output port on your monitor or computer, and then connect the left speaker to the right speaker (the cable is built into the left speaker).

There's a rubberized rotary dial on the bottom of the right speaker that controls the volume level. The dial is a little quirky as you have to press down on it slightly so the rubber will catch your finger and actually spin. I would have preferred if it was just a standard hard plastic dial but the rubberized one isn't a big deal.

As others have mentioned the volume will not get super loud if you're wanting to shake the whole house, but I did find that it is definitely louder than what my laptop can put out on it's own and plenty loud enough for casual use. Zero complaints from me on the volume level as I think anything louder would get me in trouble with my neighbors!

I'm glad I gave these speakers a shot! They are very inexpensive and met my needs perfectly!
