I am very pleased with this tiny powerhouse. I have purchased a ton of mini pc for 2 main reasons and this has stomped the competition in regards to performance and stability.
My main purpose was to setup a Debian minimal standalone kodi box to run as a Kodi media center. And this performs beautifully no lag whatsoever. I’m running debian 12.04 minimal setup without a desktop environment I have it setup from power on to Kodi screen and this is exreamly fast from bios post to Kodi. Boot live Linux and wipe windows partitions and format drive to ext4
Boot Debian 12.04 Bookworm minimal install main system when tasksel loads uncheck gnome and desktop environment after reboot
Switch to root by issuing su - not su root. Then give your user sudo rights. By installing sudo from repository by issuing apt update then apt install sudo. Now that sudo is installed. You can add your user to sudo group by issuing usermod -aG sudo kodi now kodi is my user I created during install so if your user is not Kodi change accordingly.
Next we install some basic software needed to run Kodi. From this point you can switch back to your user in my case by issuing su Kodi. Now to install the final software. sudo apt install xorg-xserver xinit dbus kodi kodi-repository-kodi -y. Wait for packages to install. Once installed we need one more command to give us the ability to use mouse and keyboard in our Kodi environment. So issue sudo usermod -aG input kodi. Remember if your user is not kodi change kodi to your user. At this point Kodi is ready to load so simply issue kodi and kodi will start. If you want kodi to auto start on boot there is a bit more work but it is quite easy to setup. There are many ways of doing this some more complex then others due to security but if your not worried about security and just want simple then it’s as easy as setting up a crontab -e and adding @reboot kodi-standalone however if you want full use of reboot or shutdown from Kodi you need to auto boot with root instead of your user. At first, it actually ran okay. For the first few months, it handled light gaming, browsing, and basic stuff decently. The RGB fans looked cool, it was quiet, and I thought, “hey, maybe I scored a good deal.”
But fast-forward to 2025, and the truth came out — this thing was built cheap from the ground up.

💣 The Ugly Truth — Why You Should NOT Buy This PC

1. Cheap, generic parts disguised as “gaming hardware.”
The listing brags about an Intel i5 CPU and Radeon RX 550 GPU, but here’s the reality:

That i5 is an older, low-power model. It’s not built for real gaming or multitasking.

The RX 550 GPU was already outdated years before this PC even shipped. It’s basically an office GPU pretending to be a gaming card.

The power supply and cooling system? Generic, no-name brands that probably cost the manufacturer $15 total. No wonder everything’s dying early.

2. Thermal disaster waiting to happen.
The system overheats constantly. My CPU runs hot, the fans struggle, and even my external monitor is starting to feel the heat. The “three RGB fans” look nice but don’t move nearly enough air. There’s no proper airflow design, and it shows.

3. No longevity whatsoever.
By 2025, this PC is coughing up its last breath. The CPU’s overheating, the SSD’s slowing down, and the fans sound like a dying lawnmower. For a system that’s only two years old, that’s pathetic.

4. Warranty and support are basically a joke.
The “one-year warranty” might as well not exist. After that, you’re on your own. Try finding replacement parts or getting actual support — good luck. Most of the components are off-brand and proprietary, so standard upgrades or replacements don’t always fit or function right.

5. False advertising at best, scammy at worst.
The way this PC is marketed on Amazon makes it sound like a mid-tier gaming rig. In reality, it’s a budget office PC dressed up with cheap RGB lights to lure beginners who don’t know the difference. If you’re hoping to play modern games smoothly — forget it. You’ll be stuck on low settings or constant crashes.

🔧 Summary — The Harsh Reality

This system isn’t “gaming-ready.” It’s barely life-ready.
If you’re tempted because it looks cool or seems affordable, don’t fall for it. You’re better off saving a little more for a real build or even buying a refurbished Dell or HP with known-brand parts.

text:
We just got some of these at work (sign company) to replace some aging computers that were not compatible with Windows 11 (it was time to upgrade to remain compliant with security updates, etc.). I’m a designer there and use Adobe apps on them. InDesign, Photoshop and Illustrator. Coming from an iBuyPower Slate MR gaming PC circa 2018/2019 with a 9th gen Core i7 processor with 16 GB RAM and an Nvidia 2080 Super graphics card (8 GB).

I haven’t noticed any issues and it seems to perform identically, except I am now on Windows 11 Pro, and this sucker is a fraction of the cost of many gaming PCs these days. I did a TON of research before suggesting these to work (and getting our IT guy’s stamp of approval).

As others have mentioned, this is not a dedicated graphics card, so be aware of that. What you are getting is onboard graphics that are much better than the old UHD 770 standard. This type of graphics processor *shares* RAM with the system. So, while it shows 128 MB VRAM for the “graphics card,” that’s not really all you’re getting. Remember that it uses the system RAM to complement that. And this thing has 32 GB of RAM out of the box. That is more than I had in my previous system, which had 16 GB of physical RAM and 8 GB on the graphics card. And it supports up to 64 GB of RAM, so the more you throw in there, the happier it’ll be.

While not a gaming PC by hard-core gaming standards (you really need a dedicated graphics card for that), I have a feeling this thing could handle some casual games (you might need to check or adjust some settings to make sure you’re maxing out your RAM utilization in-game — another comment on here mentioned a performance mode; I suspect enabling that would be what is needed to allocate enough RAM to those hungry apps). This machine supports Oculink, and connecting an external GPU basically turns it into an extreme gaming PC. All in all, the Nucbox M7 Pro packs a punch for its small size and relatively low price. The value here is crazy. I’d recommend this to anyone who wants a PC but doesn’t want to go through the hassle of building it themselves or paying a lot of $$$. text:
I ordered up 14 of these units (a couple different orders) and started installing them in client locations. Within a week, we started getting calls about the units trying to boot from PXE or saying "Operating System not found." Thought it was a fluke at first but eventually determined that this company has their own white-labeled M.2/PCIe SSDs and this series of Optiplex 7010s do NOT like them. In the end, we ended up having to replace the half dozen or so units we couldn't really swap out with new, brand-name SSDs to resolve the problem.

We did manage to return 7 of them, but I had to go buy big boxes as we'd already tossed the ones they were delivered in. Then we had to hound Amazon for several days to get the seller to actually refund the money (several days in, two of them had been refunded, but Amazon's site just kept saying "Refund in process" and they'd refund the money once they all were received). After a few pokes at Amazon, we did get our money back, but man did this cost me a lot of man hours having to rebuild failed/incompatible SSDs on the fly.

I don't know what's wrong with their white-labeled SSDs, but they must be incredibly cheap (and modern Optiplex units only really like NVMe models that can run in native RAID mode).

For the record, I did go to their web site and it looks like it was done in Microsoft Word. I managed to get a request out explaining my situation but only got a "please create a ticket" response.

I'd used OEMGENUINE in the past with good results, but wow was this a disaster. Do NOT buy these units unless you intend to put a quality SSD in it!!

Vor einem Monat habe ich den GEEKOM Mini Air 11 gekauft, um ihn in meiner Remote-Sternwarte zur Steuerung diverser Instrumente einzusetzen. Momentan läuft er im Dauerbetrieb und dient als zentrale Steuereinheit für den Empfang von Echtzeitdaten verschiedener Wettersatelliten.

Hauptgrund für meinen Kauf waren a) die zahlreichen Anschlussmöglichkeiten, b) der geringe Stromverbrauch und c) die völlig ausreichende Prozessorleistung. Bedient wird der Mini PC übrigens über Remotedesktop von meinem benachbarten Haus aus über einen LAN-Anschluss. Inzwischen habe ich auch das MS Office-Paket installiert, um mit Excel Daten auszuwerten. Auch dort stelle ich keine Leistungsminderung fest.

title: 5.0 out of 5 stars
text:
For those considering this machine, please read carefully. I selected a reseller with a price higher than the lowest offered. Why? Because at the time of my selection, the lowest price seller had 71% satisfaction rating, but for $6 more I selected another seller with a 90% satisfaction rating (TekRefurbs.com). This is especially important with a renewed computer! Many reviews reflect problems due to the differences in resellers, so it pays to select carefully.

The first thing I did on receiving the computer was open the case and remove the new 256 GB ssd, and install a 1 TB nvme ssd into the m.2 socket, and a 2 TB ssd into the hard drive caddy and reinstalled the caddy and closed the case. The computer was spotless inside and out. The next step is very important. I went to the Dell website and downloaded the BIOS update. I run linux on a multi boot system, but linux cannot install the new bios so I booted into windows for the bios update. Just follow the on screen instructions and the update takes just a few minutes. It is crucial to update the bios as the machine is vulnerable until it is done. The machcine is capable of running Windows 11, but apparently the Windows 10 Pro that comes with the computer will not allow updating. Since I did not install Windows 10, but moved my existing drives into the computer, I was all set with Windows 11. Many users prefer Windows 10.

I recommend before buying or receiving the computer that the user/owner manual in pdf format be downloaded from the dell site as it is really mandatory if you are going to get your newly renewed machine set up properly. Curiously this computer will run with either the 65 watt or the 130 watt power supply cord; mine came with the 65 watt power supply and it works flawlessy. There are also two other m.2 sockets on the motherboard for WLAN and WWAN cards as shown in the manual for those who want or need them. The cards and cables and antenna are available on Amazon.

I hope this information is useful to any who take time to read it. The machines are not for gamers as they do not have the graphics horsepower for that use, but are great for other applications if you choose the reseller carefully. It is a shame the machines suffer less than stellar ratings due to the disparities between reseller preparations. Choose wisely and you will be rewarded.
